svg.aria-label: Diagram: how AWS Network Firewall resolved IP validation works, what sets its validation scope, and the two conditions under which legitimate traffic fails the check. AWS announced that Network Firewall now supports IP validation, extending domain-based filtering beyond HTTP and HTTPS to protocols such as SFTP and SSH, by validating that a connection's destination IP address was resolved through the VPC's Amazon Route 53 VPC Resolver, closing security gaps where clients could bypass domain rules, available in all AWS commercial regions where Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall are available at no additional charge. The gap being closed is specific: a standard domain rule matches on the host name that a client asserts, the TLS Server Name Indication or the HTTP Host header, both of which the client controls. Resolved IP validation adds a check on the provenance of the destination IP address, namely whether the VPC's Route 53 Resolver returned that IP address when it resolved the domain, which closes the gap where a client sets a Host header naming an allowed domain but connects to an unrelated IP address. Because the check is based on the destination IP address rather than on an application-layer header, it also extends domain-based rules to traffic that carries no domain name at all, which is how protocols other than HTTP and HTTPS become filterable by domain. The feature works at two levels: a policy level, which verifies the Resolver resolved the connection's destination IP address for some domain and applies an enforcement action to connections that fail, and which can be used on its own; and a rule level, which matches specific domains using the AWS_ROUTE_53_RESOLVED_DOMAIN target type or the aws_route_53_resolved_domain keyword and requires the policy-level setting. The central finding concerns what sets the validation scope. AWS states that the validation scope is the set of VPCs associated with the Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rule group referenced in the policy, that every VPC associated with it contributes its resolutions to a single shared pool, and that the firewall validates against that whole pool. Critically, this includes VPCs that are associated with the rule group but do not send traffic through this firewall, and a destination IP address that any associated VPC resolved for a domain is considered resolved for all of them. The scope of what the firewall trusts is therefore set by a rule group association rather than by traffic flow, and AWS documents the consequence as an explicit warning: do not reuse that rule group for other firewalls or for unrelated deployments, because sharing a rule group across unrelated deployments widens what each firewall accepts, and a separate rule group should be used for each firewall deployment. The policy names the rule group by ID while the VPC associations that define the scope are managed separately on the Route 53 Resolver side. The second way legitimate traffic fails is Availability Zone scoping. Resolutions are recorded for each Availability Zone and validation is scoped to the zone, so a firewall endpoint validates against the resolutions recorded in its own Availability Zone. Multi-zone deployments work where routing is zone-aligned, meaning clients in a zone reach the firewall endpoint in that same zone. A connection can cross zones to reach a firewall endpoint, in which case the firewall cannot tell that the client is in a different zone, the connection fails validation as unresolved, and Network Firewall applies the configured Action to it, so with Action set to DROP that is legitimate traffic blocked for a routing reason rather than a security one. The documented exception is a firewall attached through a transit gateway, which carries the client's zone with the traffic, and AWS recommends that approach for centralized deployments inspecting traffic from multiple zones. A third condition is a cold cache, since validation recognises a destination only after the domain has been resolved through the VPC Resolver, which is why AWS gives a rollout instruction: set Action to ALERT and keep it there for about 24 hours before switching to DROP or REJECT, watching flow logs and metrics and switching to enforcement after the rate of unresolved flows settles. On evaluation timing, Network Firewall evaluates resolved IP validation once for each connection, on the connection's first packet, and the result applies for the life of the connection in the originating client-to-server direction, so a long-lived connection carries whatever verdict it received at setup. On settings, Action is required with valid values ALERT, DROP or REJECT: ALERT tags the matching connection in the firewall's flow logs without blocking it and requires that logging be enabled, so an alert-mode rollout with logging off records nothing; DROP silently blocks; and REJECT blocks and sends a TCP reset, with Reject applying to TCP while Network Firewall drops non-TCP traffic, meaning UDP is silently dropped whatever Action was chosen. A DNS expiry exception policy is required with valid values CONTINUE, DROP or REJECT, where CONTINUE treats an expired resolution as still valid, and AWS notes that resolved IP validation keeps a resolution in the resolved IP cache for longer than the DNS record's time to live, so a short TTL alone does not cause connections to fail. Source IP ranges is optional, accepting up to 100 IPv4 or IPv6 addresses or CIDR ranges, and if no ranges are specified validation applies to the firewall's VPC CIDR ranges. Changing the DNS Firewall rule group ID swaps the association asynchronously, and while a swap is in progress further changes to resolved IP validation are rejected until the policy returns to the ACTIVE state, so correcting a mis-scoped rule group is a single operation to wait on. The recommended actions are to use a dedicated DNS Firewall rule group for each firewall deployment and to list the VPCs currently associated with the rule group a policy references, since that list rather than the traffic pattern defines what the firewall accepts; to check whether routing is zone-aligned before enabling enforcement or to use a transit gateway attachment for centralized inspection; to enable flow logging and run in ALERT for about 24 hours, switching to enforcement only once the unresolved-flow rate settles; to choose the DNS expiry exception policy deliberately since it is required and CONTINUE trades strictness for availability; and to set source IP ranges if the firewall's own VPC CIDRs are not the intended scope.
svg.title: The validation scope is a rule group association, not a traffic path
svg.text: It stops trusting the header the client sends. It starts trusting a pool you may not own.
AWS Network Firewall resolved IP validation — all commercial Regions, no additional charge.
A STANDARD DOMAIN RULE
matches “the host name that a client asserts
— the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) or
the HTTP Host header”
The client controls both. HTTP/HTTPS only.
RESOLVED IP VALIDATION
adds a check on “the provenance of the
destination IP address” — did your Resolver
return it for the domain?
So it reaches “traffic that carries no domain name at all”.
But what counts as “resolved” is set by a rule group association, not by what flows through the firewall
“Every VPC that is associated with it contributes its resolutions to a single shared pool…”
“This includes VPCs that are associated with the rule group but don't send traffic through this firewall.”
AWS's own warning: “Sharing a rule group across unrelated deployments therefore widens what each firewall accepts.”
The policy names the rule group by ID. The VPC associations that set the scope are managed on the Resolver side.
Fails legitimately, 1: crossing a zone
“validation is scoped to the zone”. Cross zones and
the firewall “can't tell that the client is in a
different zone” — it “fails validation as unresolved”.
With DROP, that is good traffic blocked for a routing
reason. Fix: a transit gateway attachment.
Fails legitimately, 2: a cold cache
Validation only knows what the Resolver has already
returned, so day one looks like an attack.
“set Action to ALERT and keep it there for about
24 hours before you switch to DROP or REJECT”
ALERT “requires that you enable logging”.
Three required decisions, and one of them has no safe default to inherit
Action ALERT | DROP | REJECT REJECT is TCP only — non-TCP is dropped
DNS Firewall rule group ID rslvr-frg-... swap is asynchronous; changes rejected until ACTIVE
DNS expiry exception CONTINUE | DROP | REJECT CONTINUE “treats the expired resolution as still valid”
Before you enable it: list the VPCs associated with the rule group you are about to reference
That list, not your traffic pattern, is what the firewall will accept. “Use a separate rule group for each firewall deployment.”
Evaluated “once for each connection, on the connection's first packet” — so a long-lived connection keeps the verdict it got at setup.
